analysis.one_liner: Lets residents buy into their state's Medicaid plan as a low-cost public health insurance option.
analysis.headline: The State Public Option Act, backed by 21 senators, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced in October 2017 and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let people who don't qualify for Medicaid and aren't already insured buy into their state's Medicaid program, paying premiums capped at 9.5% of family income. Those premiums could be paid with the same tax credits and cost-sharing help the Affordable Care Act already provides. It would also raise Medicaid pay for primary care doctors to Medicare rates, give states $100 billion in grants to expand access to Medicaid doctors, and give full enhanced federal funding to states that expand Medicaid late.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured people and people paying high prices for marketplace or employer coverage would gain a cheaper, government-run insurance option in every state that chooses to offer it. People in rural or other areas where no private insurer sells silver plans would be able to use their ACA tax credits on the Medicaid buy-in. Primary care doctors, nurses, and community clinics would get Medicare-level pay for Medicaid patients, and states that expand Medicaid late would get the same enhanced federal matching funds as early expanders.

how_it_helps.text: Starting January 1, 2018, residents of a state who are not eligible for Medicaid and not enrolled in other coverage could buy into the state Medicaid plan [S2][S3].

Buy-in premiums are capped at 9.5% of family income, cost-sharing is limited to Affordable Care Act levels, and enrollees qualify for ACA premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions, with Medicaid coverage treated as a silver-level plan for credit purposes [S3].
In areas where no private silver plan is sold on the marketplace, Medicaid buy-in coverage is deemed the benchmark silver plan, so residents there can still use their tax credits [S3].

Medicaid payment for primary care services must be at least 100% of the Medicare Part B rate, covering family doctors, internists, pediatricians, obstetricians, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, certified nurse-midwives, rural health clinics, and federally qualified health centers [S3].

States may receive federal grants to improve Medicaid access to providers, with $100 billion appropriated for fiscal year 2018 [S3], and every state that expands Medicaid gets the enhanced federal match regardless of when it expands [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers would lose customers and the ACA subsidy dollars that currently flow through them, since tax credits and cost-sharing payments would go to state Medicaid programs instead. The federal government would cover 90% of buy-in administrative costs and appropriate $100 billion in access grants, borne by taxpayers. States would pay half of any buy-in premium revenue they collect beyond actual medical costs back to the federal government.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private insurers, taxpayers, and some state budgets

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates $100 billion in state access grants and a 90% federal match for buy-in administration, adding substantial federal spending that premium offsets only partly cover [S3].
Medicaid doctor networks are often narrower than private plans, so a cheaper public option could mean harder access to some specialists unless states use the new access grants to fix it [S3].
Requiring Medicare-level payment for all Medicaid primary care raises program costs and was opposed by those who argue Medicaid's lower rates are part of how the program holds down spending [S3].
The buy-in is optional for states, so coverage gains would depend on each state deciding to participate [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who can't afford marketplace plans or live where no insurer offers one, this would have been a direct, tangible option at a capped price. The main real costs are federal spending and the hit to private insurers, and the narrower Medicaid network issue is a genuine design tradeoff the bill tries to address with grants and higher primary care pay rather than solves. On balance the benefits to the uninsured and underinsured outweigh the costs, but it was never debated, so those tradeoffs were never weighed in public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Brian Schatz introduced the State Public Option Act on October 24, 2017, with 19 Democratic senators and one Independent as cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance [S1][S5].
That was the last action of any kind: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote ever occurred before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers keep the marketplace customers and subsidy dollars a Medicaid public option would have taken, and no federal money was spent on the program. Americans who lacked a low-cost coverage option gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private health insurers and the bill's opponents

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a Medicaid buy-in public option.

for.name: 20 cosponsors (19 Senate Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Booker, Harris, Sanders, Klobuchar, and Warren.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred to his committee.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor in the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 sponsors were Democrats or the Independent Sen. Sanders, no Republican cosponsored it, and the Republican-run Finance Committee and majority never acted on it [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill redirects ACA premium tax credits and cost-sharing payments from private marketplace plans to state Medicaid programs, taking customers and subsidy revenue away from private insurers. Insurers benefit from the status quo where that money flows through them.

States can enroll buy-in participants through managed care, giving these companies new paying enrollees, but the bill requires their contracts to pay primary care providers at Medicare-level rates, squeezing margins.

industries.industry: Primary care providers and community health clinics
industries.note: Medicaid primary care pay rises to Medicare rates, covering nurse practitioners, physician assistants, rural health clinics, and federally qualified health centers, and states get grants to expand provider access. Their gain runs with better access for patients.
